newsitem.title: ZAIRE: South Africans hold talks in rebel-held Zaire.
newsitem.headline: South Africans hold talks in rebel-held Zaire.

text.p: South African envoys met Zaire rebel leader Laurent Kabila on Tuesday and said Zaire was prepared for preliminary talks while in Kinshasa the government said that after dialogue it was ready to share power with the rebels until elections.
"They (the South African envoys) brought a message from Kinshasa confirming the government would participate in preliminary talks," rebel alliance justice commissioner Mwanze Kongolo said.
The vice-chairman of Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko's party said in Zaire's capital Kinshasa that the two sides would meet and "after dialogue we will share power."
"First we will talk to find the mechanism for a ceasefire and then we will share power before elections," Banza Mukalayi, vice-chairman of Mobutu's MPR party, told Reuters in Kinshasa.
The rebel official declined to say who headed the South African delegation, the first to visit rebel-held territory, but said it was not deputy president Thabo Mbeki.
Mbeki visited Mobutu in Kinshasa on Sunday in an attempt to facilitate peace in Zaire's five- month civil war.

The visit to Kisangani came as rebels from the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation Congo/Zaire (ADFL) softened their demand for face-to-face talks with Mobutu and said they were prepared to send a delegation to meet Mobutu envoys.
"We want talks Kabila-Mobutu, but before this happens there are preparatory steps in which people could work to bring the two sides together," said alliance information commissioner Raphael Ghenda.
"At a certain point the two sides could be mandated to meet to prepare a summit," Ghenda said.

Alliance rebels have seized control of around a quarter of Zaire including the third city Kisangani since the start of their campaign last October and are pressing toward the second city Lubumbashi, capital of mineral-rich Shaba region.
The rebels have consistently demanded direct talks with Mobutu in advance of a ceasefire and Kabila rejected a ceasefire request on Saturday by U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun.

Meanwhile U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan left Angola for Togo to attend an African summit on the Zairean civil war, saying he hoped progress could be made towards ending the conflict at the meeting opening on Wednesday.

"The Zairean government has insisted that a ceasefire take place before talks can begin, and (rebel leader Laurent) Kabila has said that talks must proceed before there is a ceasefire," Annan said. "I hope that in Lome we will find a basis for moving forward by perhaps having a ceasefire and talks begin simultaneously."
Both Mobutu and rebel leader Kabila have sent teams to Togo for the special summit.

The rebel drive has provoked the most serious crisis yet for Mobutu who has ruled Zaire since 1965 but is now ailing with cancer. Prime minister Kengo Wa Dondo resigned on Monday after intense political pressure connected to the collapse of the Zairean army in the face of the rebel advance.
Alliance foreign minister Bizima Karaha left Kisangani on Monday for the special Organisation of African Unity Summit on the Zaire crisis in the Togolese capital Lome.
But Karaha would use the opportunity to promote the alliance view of Zaire and its conflict rather than initiate negotiations with envoys of Mobutu, rebels said.
Karaha, yet to arrive in Lome, was flying to Togo via Goma, Kigali, Brussels and Paris, a rebel official said.

Meanwhile, Christian Monnoyer, head of the Africa desk in the Belgian foreign ministry, met Kabila in Kisangani on Tuesday to explain the presence of Belgian troops in the Congolese capital Brazzaville, according to an alliance communique.
Monnoyer said Belgian troops were stationed in Brazzaville to evacuate Belgium residents in case of need and would not intervene in the Zaire conflict, a position disputed by rebels.

"We are demanding that the international community not put soldiers in our territory because no westerners are threatened in the liberated zone and it is a threat to the integrity of our country," Kongolo told reporters.
